articles.title: Know the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke
articles.body:
As spring heats up and gives way to summer, it’s important to know the signs of heat exhaustion and heat stroke.

Heat usually peaks between noon-3 p.m. so it’s best to avoid going outdoors during these hours. If you must, try limiting yourself to short bursts. Take breaks and be sure you are well hydrated.

articles.title: Column: Living in the Already and the Not Yet
articles.author: Staff Reports
articles.body:
By April J. Buchanan | Religion Columnist

The Christian life is lived in the tension of the already and the not yet.

There are promises that are truly ours now. We have been justified, reconciled to God, and made alive together with Christ. His righteousness has been imputed to us, and our sins laid upon Him. This is not partial. It is finished.

Yet there are promises that await their full realization. We are not yet glorified or free from the presence of sin. We do not yet see Him as He is.

The Alabama High School Athletic Association announced April 15 that it is mandating a 35-second shot clock starting with the 2026-27 season.

articles.title: Opinion | America’s guardrails are eroding, and instability is growing
articles.author: Bill Britt
articles.body:
We are living through instability, and we keep telling ourselves it’s because we no longer agree.

That explanation is too easy.

Stability was built on guardrails like rules, norms and institutional restraints that forced those in power to slow down, compromise and consider consequences before acting.

For a long time, those guardrails held, even when the country didn’t agree. Over the past decade, however, we’ve begun to remove them—not all at once, but enough to change how the system behaves.

articles.title: Election 2026: Two-Term Incumbent Lashunda Scales Faces City Councilor Clinton Woods in County Commission Race
articles.body:
Primaries: Part 2 of 4

By Javacia Harris Bowser |The Birmingham Times

When Lashunda Scales was elected as the Jefferson County Commissioner for District 1 in 2018, she became the first woman to represent her district. She continued her historic tenure when she was reelected in 2022.

Now Scales will face Birmingham City Councilor Clinton Woods in the May 19 Democratic Primary.

Previously, Scales served on the Birmingham City Council, representing District 1 for three terms from 2009 to 2018.

articles.author: John A. Tures
articles.body:

articles.title: Federal court rules Alabama must use map that granted two Democrat seats
articles.author: Jacob Holmes
articles.body:
A three-judge federal panel issued a preliminary injunction Monday morning thwarting Alabama’s plan to hold new elections for Congressional districts that Republicans believed could help them gain a seat.

The U.S. Supreme Court had cleared the way for the the state to use a Congressional map lawmakers drew in 2023 despite the same three-judge federal panel finding that the map failed to remedy a Section 2 violation of the Voting Rights Act and intentionally discriminated against Black voters.

articles.title: This Matters: What are you becoming in the pursuit of power?
articles.author: Staff
articles.body:
Power reveals character, but it can also reshape it.

In politics, winning is never the only question. The deeper question is what people become while pursuing power.

Because power is temporary. But who you become stays with you.

BERLIN, Ala. –The Berlin Farmers Market will officially open for the season this Saturday,  June 6. It will be open 9 a.m.-2 p.m.

The town is encouraging families to come out to enjoy the day. Neighboring the farmers market pavilion is a playground with swings and more. There will also be a bounce house on-site with free access.

Little ones can also take part in the “POP” (Power of Produce) Club, a rewards program that allows children to engage and learn about local farmers and their produce.

articles.body:
People do not simply vote their interests. They vote their hierarchy of values.

A paycheck is an interest. So is safety, dignity, faith, belonging, liberty and the belief that your way of life deserves respect.

articles.title: CONTRIBUTOR'S VIEW - Randy Drinkard: Tomato Troubles

If you’ve noticed that your tomato plants are growing well but you don’t have many flowers, this may be a fertilizer problem. Lush, vegetative growth is usually due to over fertilizing with water soluble liquid fertilizers. Many of these liquid fertilizers are high in nitrogen which stimulates vegetative growth at the expense of flowering. articles.title: Laura Clark op-ed: Alabama spent millions on an election that 89% of voters skipped
articles.body:
Let’s call it what it is: Alabama spent millions of dollars to hold an election that only one in ten Alabamians voted in.

Last week’s runoff election drew just 408,740 voters out of nearly 3.8 million registered voters statewide. That’s barely 11% participation. Put another way, almost nine out of every ten registered voters stayed home.

Yet taxpayers still paid for polling places to open, ballots to be printed, voting machines to be deployed, and poll workers to be staffed across the state.

articles.author: Huck Treadwell
articles.body:
Three people were shot at a Brundidge nightclub in the early Saturday morning hours.

Brundidge Police Chief Ulane Jamison said the shooting happened around 1:30 a.m. Saturday morning at the Grown Folks Lounge on Highway 10.

Jamison said all three people suffered non-life threatening injuries and were transported to Troy Regional Medical Center, treated and released.

Jamison said the incident is still under investigation and no arrests have been made.

articles.title: Can Doug Jones separate himself from the Far Left?
articles.body:
Doug Jones delivered exactly the kind of Fourth of July message most Alabamians would expect from someone running for governor.

The question isn’t what he said.

It’s what he didn’t say.

As national Democrats continue making headlines with controversial rhetoric and policy positions, Jones has remained noticeably quiet about the direction of his party.

articles.title: Opinion | Algebra as a metaphor for life: what if it was never about math?

articles.title: Opinion | Where the wire stops
articles.author: David L. Albright
articles.body:
In most of Alabama, the work of building broadband looks like a trench. A crew opens the ground along a county road, lays a line, closes it, moves to the next house. Follow that line far enough and it ends at a porch, and a family that has waited years for it.

In the hardest places the line never comes. The crew stops where the cost of the next mile climbs past what the rules will pay. The house past that point gets something else: a receiver on the roof and a low-earth-orbit satellite account.

articles.title: Opinion | Every election must end
articles.author: Bill Britt
articles.body:
Some elections decide who will govern. Others test whether a nation can still govern itself.

The election of 1876 did both.

The country was only 11 years removed from the Civil War. Federal troops stood in contested states, rival governments claimed authority, political violence marred the ballot box, and Congress could not agree on who had won the presidency. The Constitution offered no clear way forward.

Occasionally, turfgrass areas begin to thin out and moss and algae start to form. These primitive plants develop because conditions for growing dense, healthy turf have declined.

Mosses are branched, threadlike green plants that form a tangled, thick mat over the soil. Algae are thread-like green plants that form a dense, green scum over the soil surface. articles.title: PREP FOOTBALL: Good Hope eyeing playoff return behind a strong veteran group
articles.body:
GOOD HOPE, Ala. –The Good Hope Raiders, led by head coach Alan Scott, rode a scorching hot offense to an 8-2 record and a playoff appearance in 2025.

With wins over Cherokee County and West Morgan, the Raiders made it all the way to the third round of the state playoffs, where they eventually fell to Plainview, 21-7.

While they’ll open their 2026 campaign with a shot at revenge over the Bears on August 21, the Raiders are mentally leaving their incredible ’25 season behind and starting fresh.

articles.title: Former Cold Springs coach Paige Adams pleads guilty: Sentenced to 7 years, will serve 1 year in prison
articles.body:
CULLMAN, Ala.– Former Cold Springs High School teacher and head girls’ basketball coach Paige Parker Adams pleaded guilty Thursday to two felony school employee sex offenses and three counts of distributing obscene material to a student.

Cullman County Circuit Court Judge Emily Johnston accepted the negotiated plea agreement and sentenced Adams, 35, to 84 months, or seven years, in the Alabama Department of Corrections.

Under a split sentence, Adams must serve 12 months in prison day for day.

In order to keep your child safe you have to educate yourself on any and all threats. One thing that can be often overlooked is button batteries. Button batteries are disc-shaped batteries that gets their nickname from their resemblance to a button or coin. They are typically 1-6 millimeters in height and 5-25 millimeters in diameter.

articles.title: What a Fall Weekend Out in Valley Actually Costs a Family
articles.author: Sponsored Content
articles.body:
The walking trail at Valley Sportsplex is finished. So is the amphitheater clearing. City officials confirmed this summer that the venue is ready for a fall music series, with the first shows penciled in for late October. For a town that has spent years watching its recreation budget get stretched thin, that's real news.

But a finished trail doesn't answer the question every Valley household asks before a Saturday: what is this weekend actually going to cost us? A walk on new pavement is free.
